prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identity of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After reading the full first round I keep a single-part B035 prize built on the discovery side, Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. The scientific case is unchanged and nobody has raised a maturity objection: proglucagon processing, the truncated active peptide and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action, receptor biology in gut, pancreas and brain, and then agonists whose benefit on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes has been confirmed in large independent trials. The Physiology or Medicine prize is best placed to recognise how the incretin system works and which peptide form is active. The drugs are the demonstration of that knowledge, and a physiology-led citation says so without naming a product. I read the chair's question about one wording that is fair to both a Mojsov trio and a Knudsen trio as answerable only partly: a citation that names both the active form and the development of therapies keeps the discovery framing and acknowledges the translation, but it cannot fix who sits in the third seat.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still the third seat and the credit around it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is publicly contested, Habener-type contributions are outside the credited names, and Knudsen, whose analogue design produced the drugs that reached patients, is left out of my trio. Round 1 did not resolve this, because every member, myself included, is working from recollection and not from verified sources in the supplied material. A trio that is seen as unfair on credit would weaken a very strong case, and the industrial character of the success makes the omission of the development leg easier to criticise. I accept these costs because the alternative, naming Knudsen and omitting the identification of the active form, leaves the discovery step unattributed in a prize about discovery.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius maintained Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation that carries GLP-1 physiology into long-acting therapy, and argued that building the prize on the contested Mojsov priority is a risk because it rests on unverified recollection.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my trio, and it moved my thinking on the citation but not on the names. You are right that none of us can verify the priority record from the files, and I said in round 1 that I would move toward Knudsen if the evidence on Mojsov proved weak. Nothing in round 1 shows that it is weak. The only new information is that five of six of us independently placed the identification of the active form at the centre of the discovery, and that is not evidence about priority. A contested claim is a reason for careful wording, so my citation names the identity of the active form and not who found it first. Your trio gives a coherent drug-development story, but it leaves the physiology of the active peptide without an attributed discoverer, and I think that is the larger gap in a prize about discovery. I would reconsider only if the committee obtains a documented record that Mojsov's contribution is not independent of Habener's.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, keeps B035 as a discovery-side trio and holds B047 as a serious alternative, while accepting that Knudsen is the strongest omitted name and that attribution is the open question.
responses.response: I agree with your reading that the Physiology or Medicine case rests on how the incretin system works and which form is active, and that liraglutide and semaglutide are engineering built on that knowledge. I also note that the chair's summary records my B047 ranking as fourth, and that is correct: I found the Walter and Mori credit the cleanest on the shortlist, but I place its medical consequence behind CAR-T, SMN2 antisense and imatinib, so I do not carry it as a second part. On your question of a second part, I do not see how to add one under the three-person cap without removing a GLP-1 name, and I will not make that trade because Drucker, Holst and Mojsov each stand for a distinct step: human physiology and secretion, receptor biology and gut-pancreas actions, and the active peptide.

responses.point: Sandberg agreed on the discovery-weighted trio, made B028 her first alternative while declining to use it as a second part, and argued that the neuroendocrine appetite actions depend on the biology Drucker and Holst described and not on analogue design.
responses.response: I agree that the appetite and satiety physiology is part of the discovery chain and is not an artefact of analogue design, and that supports the discovery-weighted trio. I also take your point that a two-part configuration would dilute what is currently a unanimous first choice. On B028 we agree it is mature and compact. My reservation, which is the one Per raised, is that the splice-site target discovery and the SMN1 gene work sit outside the credited names, and that the antisense platform consequences are still unfolding. That is why it is my first alternative and not a second part. Your answer shifts my view slightly in one respect: if the committee does want two parts, B028 would be the attribution-cleaner choice, but it would have to come with a smaller B035 credit and I would not support that.

responses.point: Perlmann treats the contested priority as a reason to examine the record and not to drop a name, and holds Mojsov as the fallback if the peptide history cannot be verified, while ranking imatinib above CAR-T on attribution and maturity.
responses.response: I agree that a contested priority should lead us to scrutinise the record and not to remove a name, and I note that it is the same reasoning I applied in round 1. On B011 versus B014 I find your comparison fair. I accepted in round 1 that BCR-ABL has a harder credit problem than it first appears, since the Philadelphia chromosome and ABL oncogene work and Novartis's role sit outside the credited trio, and your point that Eshhar is more than a footnote for CAR-T applies equally. That leaves neither as a clean second part this year. For my alternatives I keep B028 and B014, with B014 weighted by clinical effect, and I accept that its credit problem is real.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposed a physiology-led citation with a compact discovery trio, and noted that if the attribution problems prove unresolvable a cleaner candidate such as B028 with its two-person credit becomes more attractive.
responses.response: I share your concern, and it is why B028 is my first alternative. My view is that the attribution problem in B035 is limited to one seat, whereas B028 has a clean two-name credit but leaves out upstream target-site and gene discoveries. So I would not switch the prize on the strength of the Mojsov dispute alone. If the committee concluded that the priority question cannot be resolved by anyone, I would rather change the third name than change the achievement, because the physiology and the outcome trials are not in doubt. On the commercial concern we both raised, I do not use it against B035: the independent outcome trials and the academic physiology carry the case, and industry involvement is a property of how the drug reached patients, not of the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record for the active GLP-1 peptide supports Mojsov. I cannot verify it from the supplied material, and my view that the third seat should go to the active-form discoverer would change if a documented record showed her contribution was not independent.
Whether a citation can be worded to be fair to both a Mojsov trio and a Knudsen trio. I think it can acknowledge the development leg but cannot settle the third name.
Whether the absence of Habener-type contributions makes any B035 trio unfair enough to change the choice. I do not think it changes the choice of trio, but it is a real criticism of the prize.
Whether a second distinct part can exist under the three-person cap. I could not construct one without cutting a GLP-1 laureate, and I would not make that cut.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlisted ballots. I disclose a 2009 co-authorship with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons and a 2019 review co-authored with Sten Grillner, neither of which involves a shortlisted ballot. My motor-circuit expertise touches B039 and B028 only indirectly, and I have judged them on the common criteria. No recusal is needed, and my disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
